painefort.c: PAINE fort (3 dstra, in Law signifies an especial Punishment for him that being Arraigned of Felony, refuses to put himself upon the ordinary Tryal of God and his Countrey, and thereby stands Mute by the Interpretation of the Law. And is thus described by Stamford. “ He shall be sent back to the Prison, whence " he came, ane laid in some low dark House, " where he shall lie Naked on the Earth, with- “ out any latter, Rushes, or other Clothing, and “ without any Rayment about him, but only “ something to cover his Privy Members: And “ he shall lie upon his Back, with his Head co- “ vered and his Feet; and one Arm shall be " drawn to one quarter of the House with a " Cord, and the other Arm to another quarter, “ and his Legs used in the same manner ; let “ there be laid upon his Body, Iron and Stone as " much as he may bear, or more: And the next “ Day following he shall have throe Morsels of " Barly-bread, without Drink; and the second " Day he shall have Drink three times, as much " at each time as he can Drink of the Water " next unto the Prison, except it be running " Water, without any Bread : And this shall be " his Diet till he Die. This sort of Punishment, called by the Law, Paine fort (3 dure, is that which is vulgarly called, Pressing to Death.

palatum.c: PALATUM, the Palate, is the upper part of the Mouth, which because it resembles the Roof of an House, is thence called the Poof of the Mouth.

palatios.c: PALATI Os, is a small Bone almost square, it n akes the posterior part of the Roof of the Mouth : It is joined to that part of the Os Maxillare, which makes the forepart of the Palate ; it is also joined to its fellow, and the ProceJJ'us Pterigoidecus. It has a small Hole, thro' which a Branch of the fifth pair of Nerves goes to the Membrane of the Palate,

panacea.c: PANACEA, was anciently a Name given by Galen to some Medicines which he had a great Opinion of: After, by the Chymists, it was the Term for their Boasted Universal Medicine , which they pretended would Cure all Diseases in all Circumstances, Ages, and Constitutions. There are several Panacea's whole Preparation you will find in Books of Chymistry and Pharmacy ; as that of Mercury, of Antimony, &c. which perhaps may be good Medicines in many Cafes, but do all fall short of the Character of being Universal Medicines, and indeed it seems impossible there can be any such thing. The Word panacea comes from the Greeks nx* and ousiofAAi cmnia Jano. There is also a plant of this Name. l’ANARITIUM. Vid. Parcnychia, PANCHYMAGOGUES are Universal Purgative Medicines that expel all kinds of Humours j according to the ancient way of expression.

pancreas.c:
PANCREAS, the Sweet-bread, Pancration Pancrcon, Callicreas, Callicrem, and Ladles, are all Synonimous. It is a conglomerated Glandule in the Abdomen, compacted out of many Globules, or knots of Glands included in a common Membrane which ir hath from the Peritoneum ; these Globules are joined to one another, partly by Membranes, and partly by Vessels. Ic is placed behind the Ventricle, and fastened to the Gut Duodenum, and reaches from the Cavity of the Liver cross the Abdomen, to the lower end of the Spleen: By its Duct it is annexed to the Duodenum, and sometimes to the Porus Bisa - rists, to the Band Splenici, the Caul, the upper part of the Mesentery, and the upper Nervous Plexus of the Abdomen ; the Ule and Office thereof, is to convey a Volatile, Insipid,'and Lymphatick Juice, or as others will have it (for it is a disputable Point) a something acid Juice, by its own Duthis to the Gut Duodenum, in order to a farther Fermentation and Volatilisation of the Chyle, and to attemperate and allay the Qualities of the Gall: It is the biggest Glandule in the whole Body, but bigger in a Dog than a Man. Its Vessels are of five Kinds ; for it hath Veins from the Rytmus Splenicus ; Arteries Iroin. the Left Branch of the C.eliaca, and sometimes from the Splcnica. Nerves it receives from the Intercostal pair, especially from the Upper Plexus of the Abdomen. It hath also many Lymphatick Vessels, which pass as the rest do, to die common Receptable of the Chyle. Besides 5 R which Bendy.

The Pancrcatick Juice is never found in this Dud any more than Urine is found in the Ureters, by reason of the swiftness of its Motion, and the steepness of the way.

pandalea.c: PANDALEA, as the Modern Physicians call it, is the same with a Solid Electuary, but that it remains in tire, for the Sugar being rightly boiled, is let grow hard ; the Patient takes a piece of it like a Lambative; it only differs from Rolls and Morsels, as to its shape. Blanchard.

pandemius.c: PANDEMIUS,(/c. Morbus) is a Disease which is universally rife in any place. PAND 1 CULATION, is the Restlessness, Stretching, and Uneasiness that usually accompanies the cold Titos an Intermitting Feaver: ’Tis supposed to be occasioned by a Convulsive Dilatation of the Muscles, by which Nature endeavors to thro’ off something that is disagreeable to them.

panicula.c: PANICULA, is a Term in Botany, for a kind of soft Woolly Beard or String, on which the Seeds of some Plants do hang Pendulous, as in Heeds, Millet, 8cc. it signifies the same with Juba, and is opposed to Spica.

panniculuscarnosus.c: PANNICULUS Carnofus, is a flat sort of Membrane in some part thick and Musculous ; in other parts thin, with many Ducts of Fat in it, it covers the whole Body.

As suppose •her Setting, then the Angle of the 'Horizontal Parallax will be B < A " O A R, 'She knowledge of the ..'Quantity' c,'- which, is of the greatest use in Astronomy .- >-nfrom thence the Distance of the Moon, Sun, (or any other Planet) from the Earth may most easily be had • for in the Triangle BA^tAB the Semi-diameter of the Earth, B the Right Angle, and ( the Angle ot' the Parallax being known, 'tis easie ro find any Side or Angle sought, and' consequently A (, the Distance of the Moon from the Earth. This came first to be discovered by the Ancient Astronomers, thus. They observed, That the Apparent Semi-Diurnal Motion of the Moon was but 4 Degrees, whereas in reality and truth, it was 6 Degrees: Wherefore they concluded, That the Moon's Place was put forward in her Rising one Degree, and as much put backwards in her Setting ; which must needs cause her visible Motion above the Earth in 1 2 Hours, to be observed nearly 2 Degrees less, than the half of 12 Degrees, her apparent Motion in 24 Hours. Wherefore from hence they concluded the Horizontal Parallax to be just 1 Degree : Which having found, ’’twas easie to disc over ihnr A C, must be near 60 times A B, or 60 Scmi-dinmetersofthe Earth, (V: e. at 70 Miles to a Degree, and 4000 Miles the Earths Radius) 240000 Miles En gush. Mr. Auzout, gives you a, Method to find the Moon's Parallax, th\u , on a Day when she is in her Perigee, or Apogee, and in the mofi Boreal Signs, Take her Diameter towards the Horizon, and then towards the South, with her Altitude above the Horizon; the Difference of which Diameters will shew the Proportion of her Distance with the Semi-diameter of the Earth, but this is best of all done in those Places where site passes thro’ the Zenith. If the Moons Horizontal Parallax could be truly and exactly found, it would be of prodigious Advantage; for by it the Longitudes of Places on Land (and tolerably well at Sea) might be discovered. Captain Halley faith, [at the end of his Observations and Catalogue of the Southern Stars ; ) " That 'tis the want of a true knowledge of Geometry, which hath occasioned the Defects and Mistakes of Astronomers as to this Point. He there gives three ways to find the Moons Parallax, which are nearly Geometrical , of which the first seems the best ; and is thus. Let two times of Observation be taken when the Sun is (nearly) equally distant from each Node

PAR _ Node of the Moon ; and when the Moon also is to be Northerly in one Node, and Southerly in the other : In these things there needs no great Exactness, because the Differences of Latitude may be lusticiently supplied from the Tables. At these Times of Observation set the visible Places of the Moon, both in Longitude and Latitude be taken, together with her visible Altitudes and Diameters, which let be reduced to the Horizontal; then from the Times and Visible Places, let in each Observation, the Vertical Angle be computed, which is made with the Circle of Latitude at the Moons Centre ; and then the Difference by which the Southern Latitude exceeds the Northern (in our Northern part of the World) is the Sum of the Parallaxes of Latitude, which muff be divided into two parts; which to do, put into one Sum the Logarithms of the Sine of the Horizontal Semi-diameter of the visible Distance of the Moon from the Vertex, and of the Complement of the Angle of the Vertical Circle, with the Circle of Latitude, in each Observation. Then out of the greater Sum take the lesser, and to the Difference add Radius, the Sum shall be the Logarithm of the Tangent of an Ark, from whence take 45 Degrees j then will it be as Radius to the Tangent of the Remaining Ark :: So is the Tangent of the half Sum of the Parallax, to the Tangent of half their Difference : But the half Sum and half Difference together, is the greater Parallax of Latitude, and the Difference between them is the lesser. Take this Parallax of Latitude out of the visible Southern Latitude ; or add it to the Northern, and it will shew the Inclination. And then lastly, it will be as the Rectangle under the Sines of the Distance seen from the Zenith, and of the Complement of the Angle of the Vcrticle Circle with the Circle of Latitude, is to the Square of the Radius : : So is the Sine of the Parallax of Latitude, to the Sine of the Horizontal Parallax. And there is between the Sine of the Horizontal Semi-diameter of the Moon, and the Horizontal Parallax, so constant a Proportion, that if it can be but once known, the Moons Parallax at any time will be had from the Observation of her Diameter. All the Difficulty of this Process, is in observing the visible Latitudes of the Moon ; and which indeed cannot be had without the help of the Six’d Stars, whose Latitudes are in no Catalogue yet extant, correct to a Minute: Therefore the Accurate Solution of this Problem must depend on some better Tables than are yet published. And those I hope we may expect from the most Accurate Astronomer, Mr. Flamftced, when he hath sinillulhis Catalogue of the Six’d Stars, which he is now about. In the Ingenious Dr. Gregory's Aflronomia Phyftca and Geometrica, you have a great and very useful variety of Propositions for the finding the Parallax, Vide Lib. z. Sett. 7. Tho’ there be no Parallax of the Six’d Stars, in ressect of the Earths Semi-diameter, the whole Body ct the Earth being but a Point in reference to the Distance between us and the Six’d Stars : Yet in respect of the Annual Orbit of the Earth, it hath justly been expected by Astronomers, P A & that some Parallax should be found: And th|-> mt, it ur.Uoub' would be a Discovery of great Moment. could be made; because it would be antted Demonstration for the Annual Motion 01 1 Earth round the Sun, if any such Parallax co be discovered. find This the Ingenious Dr. Hoolg attempted to v observing the various Distance of a by observing the various Distance of - . ■ Star from the Zenith : (See a Dissertation 01 ^ designedly written on this Subject.) parcellingofaship.c: PARCELLING of a Ship, is laying of Pieces ot Canvase of about a Hand's breadth, over the Seams, when the is newly Calked. PAIvCEL-Airf^w, are two Officers in the Exchequer that make the Parcels of the Efcheators Accounts, wherein they charge them with every thing they have levied for the King’s Use within the Time of their Office, and deliver the same to one of the Auditors of the Court to make an Account with the Escheator thereof.

parenchymouspartsofthebody.c: PARENCHYMOUS Parts of the Body, by the Old Anatomists, arc reckoned such Fleshy Parts of it as fill up the Interstices between the Vessels, and not consisting of Vessels themselves. But by the Help of the Microscope, and more accurate Observations, it hath since been discovered, that there is no Part of an Animal Body but what is a kind of Net-work of an innumerable Quantity of small Capillary Vessels.

parenchymata.c: PARENCHYMATA, are the Intrails thro' which the Blood passes for its better Fermentation and Perfection, as the Lungs, Liver, Heart, and Spleen, GiV. Sometimes the Word Parenchyma is taken in a large Sense for all the Intrails. Blancbard.

parietalbones.c: PARIETAL Bones, or the Bones of the Synciput, are the thinnest Bones of the Cranium, iij Form almost square, somewhat long ; they arc joined to the Os Fronds by the Sutura Coronals, to one another in the Crown of the Head by the Sutura Sagittalis, to the Os Occipitis by the Lambdoidalis, and to the Ossa Temporum by the Sutura Squamefe. They arc smooth and equal on their Out-side, but on their In-side they have several Furrows made for the Passage of the Veins of the Dura me-er. They have each a small Hole near the Sutura Sagittalis, through which there pass some Veins which carry the Blood from the Teguments to the Sinus Longitudinalis,

paristmia.c: PARISTMIA, or Amygdala, arc two Glandules of the Mouth tied together by a broad slender Production ; they have one common Cavity large and oval, opening into the Mouth. The Use they serve for is, to transmit a certain slimy or pituitous Matter into the Jaws and Mouth. They are called also T on stile, which see. Blancbard.

parkoftheartillery.c: PARK of the Artillery, is a certain Place in a Camp without Cannon-ffiot of the Place besieged, where the Cannon, Artificial Fires, Powder, and other Warlike Ammunition are kept, and guarded only by Pike-men, to avoid Casualties which may happen by Fire. Every Attack at a Siege hath its Parly of Attillery.

parkofprovisions.c: PARK of Provisiotis, is another Place in the Camp, on the Rear of every Regiment, which is taken up by the Suttlcrs, who follow the Army with all sorts of Provisions, and fell them to the Soldiers.

paronychia.c:
PARONYCHIA, a Whitlow, is a preternatural Swelling in the Fingers, and very troublesome : It arises from a sharp malign Humour, which sometimes gnaws the Tendons, Nerves, the Membrane about the Bone, and the very Bone it self. Blancbard, FARO;

parotides.c: PAROTIDES, arc Glandules behind the Ears ; also a preternatural Swelling of thole Glandules.

paroxysm.c: PAROXYSM, a FA, is Part of the Period of Diseases, whereby they encrcale and grow worse. It is either Regular, which returns at certain Times, as in a Tertian or Quartan Ague; or Irregular, that has no certain Times, but comes sometimes one Day, sometimes another, as the Ervatick Ague. Blanchard. PARREL'S, in a Ship, arc Frames made of Trucks, and Ribs, and Ropes, which having both their .Ends fastened to the Yards, are so contrived as to go round about the Mails, that the Yards by their means may go up and down upon the Mails. These also, with the BreastRopes, do fasten the Yards to the Masts.

parricide.c: PARRICIDE, signifies properly him that kills his Father, and may be applied to him that murders his Mother.

parson.c: PARSON, persona, is the Law Term for the Rector of a Church ; because for his Time he represents his Church, and sustaineth the Person thereof, as well in suing, as in being sued in any Action touching the lame. Formerly he who had a Church by Institution and Induction only for his own Life, was called Parson Mortal. But any Collegiate or Conventual Body, to whom the Church was for ever appropriated, was called Parson Immortal. In the New Book of Entries, Verb. So that in Law, the Parson Impersonœ is he that hath the Poisellion of a Benefice or Rectory, be it appropriate, or otherwise, by the Act of another.

parsonage.c: PARSONAGE, or Pctlory, is a Spiritual Living composed of Glebe-Land, Tythe, and other Oblations of the People, separate or dedicate to God in any Congregation, for the Service of his Church there, and for the Maintenance pf the Minister to whose Charge the same is committed. ■ PARTES Finis nihil habuerunt, &c. in the Common Law, is an Exception taken against a Fine levied.

parties.c: PARTIES, in Law, are those which arc named in a Deed, or Fine, as Parties to it; as those that levy the Fine, and to whom the Fine is levied : So those that make any Deed, and they to whom it is made, arc called Parties in the Deed.

partitionefacienda.c: PARTITIONE Facienda, is a Writ that lies for those who hold Lands or Tenements fro indiviso, and would sever to every one his Part, against him or them that refuse to join in Partition as Copartners, &c.

partition.c: PARTITION, is a dividing of Land descended by the Common Law, or by Custom, amongst Co-heirs or Parceners, where there are two at least:; and this Partition is made Four ways, whereof Three are by Agreement, the Fourth by Compulsion. The First Partition by Agreement is, When they divide the Land equally themselves into so many Parts as they ale Coparceners, and each to choose one Share or Part, according to Order. The Second is, When they choose some of their Friends to make the Division for them. The Third is by drawing Lots, thus : Having first divided the Land into as many parts as there are Parceners, they write every part severally in a distinct Scroll, an wrapping it up, throw each of them into a Flat, Bason, or such like thing, out of which ead 1 Parcener draws one, according to their Sup cr1 ' ority; and so the Land is severally allots * The Fourth Partition, which is by Compulh 011 ' is, When one or more of the Parceners, by st’ 3, son of the Refusal of some other, lues out * Writ ot Part iti one facienda ; by Force whes c ° they shall be compelled to part. • T In Kent, where Land is of Gavel-kind P* ture, they call their Partition, Shifting. ? pastills.c: PASTILLS, are Odoriferous Tablets, or Trochiskj made up of Perfumes or Odorous Bodies, with Mucilage of Gum Tragacanth.

pate.c: PATE, in Fortification, is a kind of Platform like what they call an Horseshoe, not always regular, but generally oval, encompassed only with a Parapet, and having nothing to flank it. It is usually erected in Marshy Grounds to cover a Gate of a Town.

patee.c: PATEE, a Term in Heraldry for a Cross of this Figure the Field is Sable a Cross Patce Argent, by the Name of Croft. This Form of a Croft is called also Formee. See Molagenu, the Knee Pan.

patents.c: PATENTS. See Letters Patents. Note, That Patents differ from Writs ; and that a Coroner is made by Writ, and not by Patent.

patentee.c: PATENTEE, is he to whom the King grants his Letters Patent.

patheticknerves.c: PATHETICK Nerves, are the Fourth pair arising from the Top of the Medulla Oblongata, (and so is different from all others, which arise either from its Base or Sides) behind the round Protuberances, called by Anatomists the Nates and Tcftes of the Brain ; whence bending forwards by the Sides of the Medulla Oblongata, they presently hide themselves under the Dura Mater ; under which proceeding a while, they pass out of the Skull, each in a single Trunk, at the same Hole with the Optick Nerves, (and they communicate with no other in their whole Passage) and are bestowed entirely, as Willis faith, on that Muscle of the Eye which they call Trochlearis, because it serves to roul the Eye round about ; which being a Motion that is usually consequential upon some Passion of the Mind, such as Love, (sic. these Nerves are therefore very properly called Ocu/orum motores pathetici.

This Point is considered as Vertical to the Earth’s Centre, and is the lame with what is called the Vertex or the Zpnith in the Ptolemaic t Projection. The Scmi-diamctcf of this Path of the Vertex is always equal to the Complement of the Latitude of the Point or Place that describes it; that is, to that Place’s Distance from the Pole of the World.

pathognomonick.c:
PATHOGNOMONICK, a Term in the Art of Medicine, is a proper in separate Sign which agrees only to such a thing, and to all of that kind, and tells the Essence of its Subject, and also lasts from the Beginning to the End ; PATELLA. ME d.ji v: v

pathology.c: PATHOLOGY, is a part of Physick that teachcth us the preternatural Constitution of a Man's Body, so as thereby to discover the Nature and Causes of Diseases.

patonce.c: PATONCE. The Heralds Term for one of their Crosses of this Figure. Gules, a Crost Pat once, Argent, by the Name of La timer.

patrimony.c: PATRIMONY, is an Hereditary Estate, or Right, descended from Ancestors. The Legal Endowment of a Church, or Religious House, Was called Ecclcsinftic/il Patrimony.

patron.c: PATRON, is used in the Civil Law for him that hath manumitted a Servant, and thereby is both justly accounted his great Benefactor, and challcngcth certain Reverence and Duty of him during his Life. In the Canon and Civil Law it signifies him that hath the Gift of a Benefice ; and the Reason is, Because the Gift of Churches and Benefices belonging unto such good Men as either built, or else endowed them with some great part of their Revenue.

patrouille.c: PATROUILLE, or Patroul as we generally pronounce it, is a Round of Soldiers, to the Number of Five or Six, with a Serjeant to command them : These set out from the Corps de Cards, and walk round the Streets of a Garrison, to prevent Quarrels, Mischief, (3c. and to keep all in Order, Peace, and Quietness. pawle.c: PAWLE, in a Ship, is a small piece of Iron bolted to one End of the Beams of the Deck, close to the Capstan, but yet so easily as that it can turn about. Its Use is to stop the Capstan from turning back, by being made to catch hold of the "Whelps: Therefore they say, Heave a Pawle ! 1 hat is, Heave a little more for the Parole to get hold of the Whelps: And this they call Pawling the Capstan.

perambulationoftheforest.c: PERAMBULATION of the Forest , is the Surveying or Walking about the Forest, or the Limits of it, by Justices, or other Officers thereto appointed to set down the Metes and Bounds thereof, and what is within the Forest, and what without.

perambulationefacicndd.c: PERAMBULATIONE facicndd, is a Writ that is sued out by two or more Lords of Manners lying near one another, and consenting to have their Bounds severally known. It is directed to the Sheriff, commanding him to make Perambulation, and set down their certain Limits.

perambulator.c: PERAMBULATOR, or Walking-rchcd, is an Engine made of Wood or Iron, commonly half a Pole in Circumference, with a Movement and a Face divided, like a Clock with a long Rod of Iron, or Steel that goes from the Centre of the Wheel to the Work : There are also two Hands, which (as you drive the Wheel before you) count the Revolution, and from the Composition of the Movement, and by the Division on the Face, (hew how many Yards, Poles, Furlongs and Miles you go. The use of this Instrument is to measure Roads, Rivers, and all Level Lands, with great expedition.

perception.c: PERCEPTION, is the clear and distinct apprehension of any Object offered to us, without forming any Judgment concerning them.

perch.c: PERCH, a Measure by our Statute Law of 16 Foot and an half in Length. See Pole.

perdonatioutlagarue.c: PERDONATIO utlagar'ue, is a Pardon for him who for.Contempts in not coming to the King’s Court, is Out-law’d, and afterwards of his own accord, yieldeth himself to Prison.

peremptory.c: PEREMPTORY, in Law, signifies a final and determinate Act, with put hope of renewing or altering.

perfectnumbers.c: PERFECT Numbers, arc such whose Aliquot or even parts -.spin’d together, will exactly return the whole' .Number, as 6 , 28, < 3 c. for of six, the half is three, the third part two, and the sixth part one, which added together, make six; and it hath no more aliquot parts in whole Numbers : So twenty eight, which has these parts, i 4 > 7 , 4, 2, and 1, exactly return 28 ; which therefore is a Perfect Number, whereof there is but ten between one and one Million of Millions.

petrifaction.c: PETRIFACTION, is properly the changing of a rnix’d Body into a Stony Substance, when it had no such Nature before ; and the Action by which this is performed, is called,

petrification.c: PETRIFICATION, and the Thing so changed, is said to be Petrified. ’Tis justly questionable, Whether there be any such thing as this in Nature, or not ? Petrifaction indeed now adays, is a mighty modish Word, for every thing almost that is found upon the Surface, or dug out of the Earth, pastes with some Persons by this Name. But what is there that really and truly deserves the Name of a Petrifaction ? When the Petrifying Waters, as they arc called, (which are nothing but Waters impregnated with a great deal of Stony Matter, which in their Passage through the Earth became dissolved in them: ) When these, I say, incrust ate Rustics, Grafs, or Sticks all over with a Stony Coat, by letting the Stony Particles dissolved in them, by little and little, fall down upon and adhere to them ; or it may be Insinuate into their Pores, and deposita themselves there : And when after this, the Vegetable part inclosed, rots and moulders away, and the Stony Coat, or Substance daily increases; this is not the Transmutation of a Vegetable Substance into a Stony or Mineral one, and therefore the new Body thus formed, is not properly a Petrifaction in the true Sense of the Word. And when many Bodies arc found in the Earth, which by all possible ways of judging and distinguishing, approve themselves to be Animal or Vegetable Bodies, such as the Shells, 1 etch, Bones of Animals, the Fossil Trees, Pine, Cones, Hazel Nuts, Cc. which arc every where found deep in the Earth. It appears odd to call these Petrifactions, and more odd to suppose them nothing but the Sperlings of Nature ; and to affirm all these things to be nothing but nicer Formed Stones, only because we cannot account presently how they came thus into the Earth, or rather don’t like that any others are able to account for it: Bur every one will have his own w ay of Expression.

phosphorus.c:
PHOSPHORUS, a Chymical Preparation* which being exposed to the Light or Air, will seine in the Dark. Of this there are several kinds, whose Process shall be briefly delivered. T o make the Bolonian Phcjphorus, see under the Bolonian Stone. The most Common Way (with us) is to make the Phosphorus from Human Urine. And the Hint came first by Chance thus : One Brand , an Alchymist of Hamburgh, wisely thinking to find the Philosopher’s Stone in Human Urine, workt upon it in a Retort, and so forced over the Phcjphorus Matter; yet he would not communicate this Discovery to any one, and so the Secret died with him. After his Death, one Kirhkplius a Saxon Chymist set himself to find it out, (having heard of such a thing) and succeeded accordingly ; and this Man shewed the Process to several of his Friends. The Honourable Mr. Boyle having (in part) had an Account of this Pbejphorus, from one Daniel Kjajf, a. German, about the Year 1680 publisecd in Englijh an Account of the Way of making this Phojphorus, and several very Curious Experiments upon it, under the Title of Noftiluca. And since that, Mr. Horn berg hath written largely about it, as you may fee in the Memoirs (for the Months March and April ) of the Royal Academy of Sciences at Parts, 1691. The Way of Preparing it, is this - Take a good large Quantity of the New-made Urine of Bcer-drinkers, and evaporate it gently, to the Consistence of Honey : Then put it in an Earthen Vessel, cover it, and place it in a Cellar for three or four Months, that it may throughly ferment and putrific. Then mix a double Quantity of Sand, or Ponder of Pots, with one part of this corrupted Urine, and put it into an Earthen Retort or Glass one coated; and fitting it to a large long-neck’d Glass Receiver, in which was before put two or three Quarts of Water, distil it in a naked Fire, in a Reverberator)'Furnace, gently at first, for about two Hours; afterwards augment the Fire gradually, 'till all the Volaril Salt and black Foetid Oil be drawn off. Then raise the Fire to the highest Degree, and white Clouds will come into the Receiver, and six to it by little and little, on one side of it, in the form of a yellowish Skin, and another parr will precipitate to the bottom in Pouder. Keep the Fire thus violent for three Hours, 'till no more Fumes will come. Let all cool, -md unIute the Vessels; and throwing more Water into the Receiver, shake all well about, to loosen what will stick to the sides; and then pour it all into a large Glass Vessel, where it will fettle ; rhe Vblatile Salt will dissolve in the Water, but the Phcjphorus and the Oil will sink to the bottom. Pour off the Water, and gathering the remaining Matter together, put it into a little Glass Vessel, with a little fresh Water, and digest it in a Sand-heat, stirring the Matter about from time to time with a Wooden Spatula ; the Phojphorus

P H O P M Y Phosphorus ' by this means vviil separate from the Oi), and sink to the bottom. Pour away the Oil, and make the Phosphorus up,- while hot, into little Sticks or Pieces, which must be kept in ft Viol of Witter close stbpt. : This is the Solid Phosphorus, with which, if you write any Letters on Paper, or on a Wall, they will appear Luminous in the Dark, and continue so a good whiles If you cut off a little bit of it, and rub it strongly along a piece of Paper, with a Knife, it will actually enkindle the Paper. The Liquid Phofjihcrus' is made by digesting in Horso-dung a little bit, or some Scrapings of she Solid, sot two Days, in Oil or Essence of Cloves, Oil of Turpentine, (3 c. For after 4 t is dillblvcd in the Ot!, it will impregnate it so,that as toon as ever you open the Bottle, the Matter Wd.ll appear all iu ti Flame/ •' If you put a little of the Solid Phosphorus into a Viol, with a little Oil of Vitriol, that is very strong and well dephlcgmated, and then add to it about half as much common Water as there \vAs Oyl of Vitriol, the Mixture will grow very hot, and fiubak; and it you carry the Viol into the Dark, you will sec the Phosphorus enkindled, and sparkle in many places os'the Viol, like Meteors, or little Falling-stars : And if a small Quantity of Oil of Turpentine be added, it will produce an actual Flame. Lemery mentions a Ncw-invented Phojphorus of Mr. Homberg s, being made of one part of Salt Armoniack, and two of Quick-limc slackt by the Air; which arc fluxed together in a Crucible, into a kind of Gray Glass, which when it is struck with a Hammer, appears presently of a light Fire. Phojphorus Batduini, called the Hermetic^ Phosphorus, is tlius made : Heat red-hot about two pounds*of Chalk, let it cool, and ponder it. Then take a pint of Aquafortis, and put into it a-spoonful of your pondered' Chalk; a great Ebullition will arise : Repeat this dill the throwing of the Ponder makes no Ebullition at all. After this, let the Liquor fettle, and decant it into an Earthen Pan placed in Sand, and evaporate all the Liquor, so there will remain a kind of Salt at the bottom. Put this Salt into a Coppcl, or a strong Farthen unglazed Pan ; set it in a gentle Sandhcar, and the Matter will swell. Continue this gentle Fire ’till it be funk down a little towards the bottom ; then cover the Pan or Coppcl with a Lid that .hath two or three Holes in it, and encrcale the Fire gradually, ’till it be strong enough to melt the Matter; and when ’tis melted, a yellow Vapour will exhale through the Holes in the Cover. Then take the Vessel presently off the Fire, and putting on another Earthen Lid, which hath no Holes in it, set it by to cool. Round about the sides ot the Pan you will find a Crust of yellow Matter, that is the Phosphorus : It must sic kept in a Box well stopt, in a dark place. When ’tis design’d to berendred Luminous, you must expose it, like the Pol avian Stone, to the Light, for a small Space; and then removed into the Dark, it will thine there. If k be left in the Dark, exposed to the Air for about Fifteen Days, it will thine all that wlnap but after that, go out, and never be Luminous more. pinionofreport.c: PINION of Report, is that Vinion in a Watch, which is commonly fixed on the Arbor of the Great Wheel, and in old Watches used to have commonly but four Leaves ; it driveth the Dial tVhecl, and carricth about the Hand. The Quotient or Number of Turns to be laid upon the Pinion of Report, is found by this Proportion ; as the Beats in one Turn of the Great Wheel, to the Beats in an Hour : So arc the Hours of the Face of the Clock, (vi%. 12, or 24-) to the Quotient of the Hour Wheel, or Dial Wheel, divided by the Pinion of Report, i. e. the Number of Turns which the Pinion of Report hath in one Turn of the Dial Wheel: that is, in Numbers, 26928 : 20196 . 12 : 9. Or rather thus. As the Hours of the Watch's going, are to the Numbers of the Turns of the Fufy :: so are the Hours of the Face, to the Quotient of the Pinion of Report. If the Hours be 12, then 16 : 12 :: 12 : 9. Butif 24, the Proportion is 16 : 12 :: 24: 18. N. B. This Rule may serve to lay the Pinion of Report on any other Wheel, thus : As the Beats in one Turn of any Wheel to the Beats in an Hour :: So are the Hours of the Face, or Dial Plate of the Watch, to the Quotient of the Dial Wheel divided by the Pinion of Report fixed on the Spindle of the aforesaid Wheel. 1

PLAIN Sailing, is the Art of finding all the Varieties of the Ships Motion on a Plain, where all the Meridians are made Parallel, and the Parallels at Right Angles with the Meridians, and the Degrees of each Parallel equal to those of the Equinoctial; which, tho’ notoriously false in it self, supposing the Earth and Sea to be a Plain Flat, and each Parallel equal to the Equinoctial ; yet by laying down Places accordingly, and breaking a long Voyage into many short ones, a Voyage may pretty well be perform’d by it, near the same Meridian. We now number the Earth among the Primary Planets, because we know it moves round the Sun, as Saturn, Jupiter., Mars, Venus, and Mercury do, and that in a Path or Circle between Mars and Venus. And the Moon is accounted among the Secondary Planets, or Satellites of the Primary, since site moves round the Earth, as Jupiter % Four Moons or Satellites do round him, and Saturn's Five round about him; if Cajsmi’s Eyes may be credited. But I could never fee my self, or meet with any one else who ever did see any but the Hugenian Satellite. All the Planets, as far as we can find, have, besides their Motion round the Sun, which makes their Year j also a Motion round their own Axes, which makes their Day; as the Earth’s revolving so, makes our Day and Night. It’s more than probable that the Diameters of all the Planets arc longer than their Axes: We know ’tis so in our Earth ; and Mr. Flamjlead and Mr. Cajswi both found it to be so in Jupiter. And therefore ’twas a great Mistake in the Ingenious Dr. Bi/met, to assert, as he doth in \m Hypothesis, the Polar Diameter of the Earth to exceed the other. Mr. Isaac Newton asserts our Earth's Equatorial Diameter to exceed the other by about 34 Miles: And indeed else the Motion of the Earth would make the Sea rise so high at the Equator, as to drown all the Parts thereabout. For when that determinate Degree of Velocity, which ac one Distance were just Commensurate to the Central Bodies Attraction, and so would produce a Circular Orbit, must at a farther Distance be too hard for it, by reason of the Diminution of the Attraction there ; an Elliptical Orbit must be described, whose nearer Focus would be coincident with the Central Body. In like manner, when the same determinate Degree of Velocity were at a nearer Distance, where the Central Arrraction is augmented, it would be too little for the same - and an Elliptical Orbit must be described, whose farthest Focus would be coincident with the Central Body. This cannot be difficult, if you consider, rhat the Species of the Planetary Orbits depend soly on the Proportion between the Attraction towards the Central Body, and the Velocity of the Projectile Motion ; as that Proportion remaining at any Distance whatsoever, the Bigness of the Orbits will be various, but the Species the same : So when that Proportion is changed, the Species of the Figures must be chang’d also; which being done, the Velocity given, by the various Force of Attraction in several Distances from the Centre, as well as by the various Velocities at a given Distance, of which before ; ’ris evident the Species of the Orbits will be different in this as well as in the former Cafe. And the greater Disproportion there is between the Quantity of Attraction and the Velocity of the Revolving Bodies, the farther from ' a Crisp L A P L A b L ircu'ar; and the more Oblong and Eccentrical will the Orbits described be. And the greater Approach to Correspondence there is, the nearer to Circular, and the less Oblong and Eccentrical will the same Orbits be. The Circular Orbits of Planers depend not only on the exact > Adjustment of the Projectile Velocity to the Attractive Power of the Sun, but upon the Direction of the lame Projectile Morion, at the Original Commencing of the Attraction. Thus where the Planet is in its own Tangent, neither Ascending nor Descending, and the Angle preceding C B A is a Right one, which we have hitherto supposed; from the Correspondence of the Velocity to the Attraction, the Orbits will be perfect Circles. Otherwise, when the Direction of the Motion is Oblique, in any measure ascending from or descending to the Central Body, and the preceding Angle C B A Obtuse or Acute; the Planet, tho’ its Velocity were exactly adapted to the Attraction of the Central Body, would revolve in an Ellipsis ; and the Point B, where the Attraction began, would be the End of the lesser Axis thereof. pleonasmus.c: PLEONASMUS, is a Figure in Discourse, when a Word not necessary is added, to express a Vchcmcncy in us, and a greater Certainty in the thing ; as when we say, 1 Jaw it with these Eyes : Here, saw it, is really enough in Grammar, but with these Eyes, is added, to Shew both the Certainty of the Fact, and our Zeal and Vehemence in asserting it.

plerotica.c: PLEROTICA are Medicines that breed Flesh and fill up Wounds.

plethora.c: PLETHORA, when there’s more good Blood than is requisite: It happens either to the Vessels, when they are stretch’d out, and cannot hold all ; or the Strength, for sometimes tho’ the Vessels be not over full, the Strength is overloaded.

plevin.c: PLEVIN, in Common Law, signifies a Warrant, or Assurance. Sec Replevin.

pleura.c: PLEURA, is the Skin or Membrane which covers the inside of the Thorax, adhering to the Ribs.

pleuritis.c: PLEURITIS, a Pleurisic, is an Inflammation of the Membrane Pleura, and the Intercostal Muscles, attended with a continued Fever, and Stitches in the Side, Difficulty of Breathing, and sometimes Spitting of Blood ; and it’s either a true Pleurisic, this which we have described, or a Bastard Pleurisic, whole Symptoms are not so violent, and in some things different from the former.

plexuschoroides.c: PLEXUS choroides seems to hang over the Pineal Glandule, as it were over a Button. It is an admirable Contexture of small Arteries in the Brain like a Net.

plexusnervosm.c: PLEXUS Nervosm, is when two or three Nerves meet together and jut out.

plica.c: PLICA, is an Epidemical Disease in Poland , when their Hairs grow together like a Cows Tail ; besides, they are Crooked-back’d, have loose Joints, it wrenches their Limbs and loosens them, breeds Lice, with other Symptoms.

plinthusorplinthis.c: PLINTHUS or Plinthis, in Architecture, is taken for that Square Member which serves as a Foundation to the Base of a Pillar : But Vitrtivius calls the upper part, or Abacus of the Tuscan Pillar, a Plinth, because it resembles a square Tile. Moreover, the same Denomination is sometimes attributed to a thick Wall,, wherein there are two or three Rows of Bricks advanced in form of a Plat-band. This PLINTH Pah ado calls the Orte, and Blondell the Alacus. The Word is also used for a like Member about the Capital of a Pillar, but then 'tis called always the Plinth of the Capital, and is placed just above the Echinus in the Dorics, and above the Ovolo, or quarter Round in the other Orders.

In Corn it is that part, which after the Pedicle is shot forth, shoots out towards the smaller end of the Seed, and therefore is by some called the Acrofpire .

pluries.c: PLURIES, is a Writ that goeth out in the third place, after two former Wtits that had no effect.: For first the Original Capias issues, and if that speed not, then goeth out the Ainu, and if that also fails, then the Pluries.

pneumatickengine.c: PNEUMATICK Engine, the same with the Air Pump.

pneumatocele.c: PNEUMATOC ELE, is a Windy Rupture, when the Skin of the Scrotum is distended with ."Wind.

pneumatomphalus.c: PNEUM ATONIPHALUS, is a Swelling in the Navel, got by Wind.

pneumatosis.c: PNEUMATOSIS, is the Generation of Animal Spirits, which is performed in the Cortical Substance of the Brain ; the little Arteries there are emptied, and the Spirits distil, which after they are come as far as the middle of the Brain, they Actuate and Invigorate all the Nerves.

podagra.c: PODAGRA, vid. Arthritis, The Gout in the Feet.

pole.c: POLE, in Measuring, is the same with Perch or Upd, or as some call it,Lugg. By our Statute Law, {Ann. 35 Eli^.Cap. 6.) this Measure is a Length of 16 Feet and an half, but it varies by the Usage of some Countries3 being so some ces of 18 Feet, which they call Woodland Measure ; in some places of 21 Feet, which is called Church Measure ; (/’. e. of such Lands as did or do belong to the Church ) and in others ot 24 Feet, and this is called Forreil Measure.

polestar.c: POLE Star, is a Star in the Tail of the Lit' tie Bear, (a Constellation of 7 Stars which is called Cynosure) and is very near the exact North pole of the World. The right Ascension of this so/e Star for this Year 1700, is o Hours 35 Minutes 0 Seconds of Time ; and it Increases 1 Mijmite 16 Seconds every 1 o Years: Therefore having at any time this Stars Right Ascension, and the Right Ascension of the Sun (both in time) if you Subtract the latter from the former, (adding 24 Hours to the Right Ascension of the PoleStar when it is iels than the Suns) the Remainder will he the Time when the Pole Star is in the Meridian. Then Hang up two Strings and Plummets between the Pole Star and your Eye, and you will have a true Meritlian Line, which wil} be of great tile to rec tisic a Clock or Watch; And you may sincl the Meridian very nicely, if instead of the Strings above mentioned, you use the Sights of a good Circumfercnter, or other Surveying Instrument. Some Persons have been mighty apt to imagine, That the Height or Elevation of the Pole, and also the Position of the Circles of the Heavens, in respect of those on the Earth, hath much changed and varied: But Mr. Cast'mi is doubtless right in his Assertion, That there is no just ground for any such Surmise : And that all the Difference which we find now in the Latitudes of Places, G?c. in respect of the Ancient Accounts, arises from the former Observations not being well made; as indeed we may judge they cannot have been, since they had no such good I Instruments to do it withal, as the Modem Astronomers have. Yet he thinks it very probable, that there may be some little Variation in the Height of the Pole, in one and die same place ; but this not exceeding two Minutes, and which will in process of Time quite vanish, after ’tis arrived to its highest Difference. Vid. Mcmoires de Mathemat. & de Physique, July 1693.

poleofaglass.c: POLE of a Glass (in Optickj) is the thickest part of a Convex, but the thinnest of a Concave Glass, and if the Glass be truly ground, will be exactly in the middle of its Surface: This is sometimes called, T he Vertex of the Glass.

polesoftheworld.c: POLES of the World, arc two Points in the Axis of the Equator, each 90 Degrees Distant from its Plane ; one pointing North, which therefore is called, The North or Article Pole ; the other Southward, which therefore is called, The South or Antartick_ Pole. Whether any People live directly under the Pole or not, is a Question ; but Mr. Ha Hey hath proved, That the Solstitial Day, under the Pole, is as hot as under the Equinoctial, when the Sun is Vertical to them, or in their Zenith ; because for all the 24 Hours of that Day under the Pole, the Suns Beams are inclined to the Horizon with an Angle of 23 a Degrees : Whereas under the Equinoctial, tho'he become Vertical, yet he shines no more than 12 Hours, and is absent 12 HoursAnd besides, for 3 Hours 8 Minutes of that 12 Hours he is above the Horizon there, he is not so much Elevated as under the Pole.

pompholigodes.c: POMPHOLIGODES, Urine with many Bubbles upon it; which are frequent, if the Body be putt up or pained. Blanchard.

pomumadami.c: POMUM Adami, is a Protuberance in the Fore-side of the Throat; so called, because 'tis foolishly thought a piece of the Apple stuck in Adams Throat, as part of his Punishment, and hence derived to his Posterity. Blanchard. In Reality ’tis only the Convex part of the first Cartilage of the Larynx , called Scutiformis. This is greater in Men than in Women.

pone.c: PONE, is a Writ, whereby a Cause depending in the County Court, or other Inferior Court; is removed into the Common-Pleas. "PONE fer vadium, is a Writ to the Sheriff to take Surety of one for his Appearance ac a Day assigned.

ponendisinaffifis.c: PONENDIS in Affifis, is a Writ founded upon the Statute of H-'esitn. 2 cap. 38. and upon the Statute Articuli Super Chartas, cap. 9; Which Statutes shew what Persons Sheriffs ought to impannel upon AJJIses and Juries, and what not.

ponenduminballium.c: PONENDUM in Ballium, is a Writ commanding a Prisoner to be bailed, in Cases Bailable.

ponendumsigillumadexceptionem.c:

ponscerebri.c: PONS Cerebri, ( by some) is a Congeries or Heap of innumerable Filaments divaricated out of the Solider Substance of the Brain, whence all the Nerves take their Rife.

pontage.c: PONTAGE, is a Contribution towards the Maintenance or Re-edifying of Bridges. It may al Ib fignitic Toll taken to this Purpose of thole that pass over Bridges.

pontibusreparandis.c: PONTIBUS l(eparandis, is a Writ directed to the Sheriff, esc. willing him to charge one or more to Repair a Bridge, to whom it belong th.

ponton.c: PONTON, in Fortification, is a Bridge made of two Boats, at some Distance one from another, both covered with Planks ; as also the Internal Space betwixt them. They have Props and Rails on each side; and the whole Structure ought to be so solid, as to be able to transport the Horse, together with Cannon and Baggage, as well as the Infantry.

pontvolant.c: PONT Volant, or the Flying Bridge, used in Sieges, is made of two small Bridges laid one over another ; and so contrived, by the means of Cords and Pulleys placed along the sides of the Under Bridge, that the Upper can be pushed forwards ’till it joins the Place where it is to be fixed: But however the whole Length of both these Bridges must not be above Four or Five Fathom long, lest they should break with the Weight of the Men. These are chiefly used ro surprise Out-works or Posts that have but narrow Moats.

poopofaship.c: POOP of a Ship, is die Floor or Deck over the Round-house or Master’s Cabbin, being the highest part or uppermost part of her Hull af ern.

popliteavena.c: POPLITEA Vena, is the Vein of the Ham, and sometimes reaches down the back of the Leg even to the Heel. This comes from the shad al Branches of the Vena Cava ; which, after they descend as low as the Thighs, are called Crurales.

popliteus.c: POPLITEUS, by some called Subpopliteus, is a Muscle of the Leg, which ariseth with a short strong Tendon from the External Head of the Inferior Appendix of the Os Femoris ; from whence descending obliquely over the Juncture, becomes Fleshy, and expanding it self, is so inserted to the Superior part of the Tibia internally, immediately below its Superior Appendix. This assists the other Muscles in bending the Tibia, and also Antagonizeth the Biceps, by turning the Foot and Toes outwards when we sit with our Knees bended.

pores.c: PORES, are small Interstices, Spaces, or Vacuities between the Particles of Matter that constitute every Body, or between certain Aggregates or Combinations of them. Thus, for Instance, those little imperceptible Holes in the 'Skin, thro’ which the Sweat and Vapours insensibly breath out of the Body, arc called Pores $ *"d the having of such Holes or For es in any Body, is called Porosity or Porousnesi. I he Honourable Mr. Boyle has written a Particular Essay on the Porosity ot Bodies; in which he proves, That the most Solid Bodies that are have some kind of Peres. And indeed, if they had not, all Bodies would be alike Spoclfi^d weighty.

POSITION, or the Pule of Position, otherwise called the Rule of Falfhood, is a Rule in Arithmetics, wherein any Number is taken to work the Question by, instead of the Number sought; and so by the Error or Errors found, we find the Number required. This Rule of False Position is of Two kinds,' vi%. Single and Double.

POTENTIAL Coldness, is a Relative Quality which some Drugs, Simples, or Compound Medicines are supposed to be endowed with : And therefore you will find frequently in some Old Books, or in the Writings of such as follow the Old Physicians, that such a Plant or Drug, is cold in the id or 3d Degree: The meaning of which is, not that such a Plant is actually Cold to the Touch, but that it is Cold in its Effects and Operations, if taken Inwardly. And whenever such an Effect doth follow the taking of such a Medicine, Mr. Boyle thus accounts for it according to the Mechanical Philosophy, ©sis. That this Body, which they call Potentially Cold, is made up of Corpuscles of such a Size, Shape, 0c. that being disjoined and resolved by rbe Menflruum of the Stomach, or the Fluids it may elsewhere meet with, they do so associate themselves with the small parts ot the Blood and other Liquors, as by clogging and impeding them to lessen their wonted Agitation; and perhaps also to make them act in a peculiar way, as well as less briskly on the Nervous and Fibrous parts of the Body : The Perception ot which bmminution, or perhaps Change ot Motion in the Organs of 6 A Feeling,

P o w P R A Feeling, is that, which being referred to the Body .that produced it, is called Potential Coldness. Hence, if it be supposed that in Agues some Morbifick Matter of a viscous, or not easily dissipable Texture, be harboured in some part of the Body, and requires such a Time to be made find and resolvable, which is an Hypothesis generally received, the Cold Fits in these Diicaics, wil! be plausibly accounted for. Also the Shiverings and Cod arising from the taking of molt Poisons, may hence be solved ; and that Icsler Degree of it which seizes Hypochondriacs and Hyjlericttl Persons.

Whatever is gotten out of of a Menstruum, in which it was dissolved, and by some means is precipitated o f made fall down to the bottom of the Vessel, may properly be called Precipitate. See Precipitation. But the Chymists and Writers of Pharmacy commonly give this Name by way of Eminence to the Mercury dissolved in Acid Menstruums, and then afterwards precipitated down to the bottom in fine Ponders of which they reckon these following: 1. White Precipitate, which is Mercury dissolved in Aqua-fortts ; or, which is better, Spirtt of Nitre ; and then precipitated to the bottom with Salt Water, and a little Spirit of SalArmoniack. But if instead of Salt Water, and that Volatile Spirit, you had used hot Urine, a Ponder would have fallen down, which may be called, 2 . Epste Precipitate, since it will be of a Pale Rose Colour. 3. Red Precipitate, is Mercury dissolved in Spirit of Nitre, and then the Moisture is evaporated in a Sand-Heat; and then the Fire being gradually encrcascd to the Third Degree, the Matter turns Red. Tho’ this be called a Precipitate, ’tis improperly so here, being no Precipitation at all. If Spirit of Vitriol be dropr into a little of this Red Precipitate, it presently turns it White ; but Spirit of Sal-armoniack will turn it Grey. There is also another sort of Red Precipitate which the Chymists call Philosophical Precipitate, and often Precipitate per se ; which is by including Running Mercury in a Matrass, which is set in a Sand-Heat for Forty Days ; or’till all the Mercury be reduced to a Red Ponder. 4. Green Precipitate, is made by mingling the Dissolutions of Mercury and Copper together, both made in Spirit of Nitre ; the Mixture is evaporated to Dryness, and then the Mass at the bottom is pondered, and hath distilled Vinegar poured upon it, and digested with it for Twenty four Hours, or ’till the Liquor looks Green, and a little Blewislt; then the Liquor is poured off, and more Vinegar put on, and so repeated ’till all be dissolved : Then all these Dissolutions are mixed and evaporated in a Sand-Heat ’till the Matter be of the Consistence of Honey ; then taken off the Fire, it will harden as it cools, and grow pulverizable. . The Ponder of it is this Green Precipitate, as improperly so named as the other Red ones. . 5 . Yellow Precipitate. See Turbith Mineral. If Sublimate Corrosive be dissolved in Water, a little Oil of Tartar, per Deliquium, poured into the Solution, will make a Red Precipitate ; and Spirit of Sal-Armoniack will give from some more of the same Solution a White Precipitate ; and Lime-water will give the Solution a Yellow Colour, as you may see in that Phagcdenick. Water : And a little Spirit of Vitriol will clear off these Precipitates, and Colours, and render the Liquor greatly transparent and colourless like Fair Water. All

PRE PRE AU these Precipitates, or any other, may easily be revived into Running Mercury, by mixing them with Quick-Iimc, and then distilling, as in Reviving Mercury from Cinnabar ; which lee.

precipitation.c: PRECIPITATION, in Chymistry, signifies the Fa!Iing-down of the Particles of any Metalline or Mineral Body, which are kept suspended in that Menstruum which dissolved it, by the pouring in of some Alkahfate, or other contrary Liquor, or. by putting something else into it, which is more easie for the Menstruum to dise solve. Thus if Silver be dissolved, and its Particles kept suspended in Aqua-fortis, Spirit of Nitre, (3c. some Oil of Tartar per Dehquium ) or even Salt Water, will presently make the Acid let go the Silver, and it will fall down or precipitate to the bottom in a White Pouder: Or if into the Solution of Silver you had put a Plate of Copper, this Metal being easier to work upon than the Silver, the Acid will fall to dissolving of it, and consequently let go the Silver, which will soon precipitate or fall down to the bottom, and cover the Copper Plate all over with White Scales. See the Word Depart. Mr. Boyle defines Precipitation in General to . be an Agitation or Motion of an Heterogeneous Liquor, which in no long time will make the Parts of it subside, and that usually in the Form of a Pouder or other Consistent Body. This Noble Gentleman proposes, That the Corpuscles contained or kept suspended in any Solvent or Menstruum, may be precipitated down by either or both of these two General ways : i .By adding to the Weight or Bulk of the dissolved and floating Particles, and thereby rendering them unfit any longer to accompany the Particles of the Menstruum in their Intestine Motions: Or, idly, by weakening the Sustaining Power of the Menstruum, and thereby disabling it to keep the dissolved Particles from swimming any longer in st. See more in his Excellent Discourse upon the Mechanical Causes of Precipitation.

priminglow.c: PRIMING low, is a small sharp Iron which is thrust into the Touch-hole of a Great Gun, and pcirces into the Cartridge that holds the Ponder, that so they may put in the Primc-pou der or Touch-pouder to site off the Piece.

primogeniture.c: PRIMOGENITURE, in Law, is the Title of an Elder Brother in Right of his Birth.

primoresdentes.c: PRIMORES Dentes, feu lncisivi Dentes, arc the Four Foremost Teeth in each Jaw ; they are pretty broad, sharp at their Ends, a little convex outwards, and hollow inwards ; they have each a pretty long Root, a little crooked, and divided into two, by which means they have the greater Force in cutting off the Aliments, which is their proper Use. PR I MUM Mobile, in the Ptolemaic ^ Astronomy, is supposed to be a vast Sphere, whose Centre is that of the World, and in Comparison of which the Earth is but a Point: This they will have to contain all other Spheres within it, and to give Motion to them, turning its self and all them quite round in Twenty four Hours.

principal.c: PRINCIPAL, in Common Law, signifies the same with Heirloome.

principle.c: PRINCIPLE, a Word very commonly and very variously used ; sometimes it signifies the same as a Maxim, an Axiom, or a good Practical Rule of Action .- Thus we say, a Person is a Man of Principles, when he always acts according to the Eternal Rules of Morality, Virtue and Religion. Sometimes it signifies a Thing Self-evident, and as it were Naturally known, and then tis usually called, a First Principle ; as that, Nothing can Esfift and not Exiil at the same time : That, Hfioere there is no Law, there is no Tranfgrejficn: That a Whole is greater than a Part, Somep k i P R I_ Sometimes it hath the lame sense with Rudiments or Elements ; as when we say, the Principles of Geometry, Astronomy, Algebra ; we mean the Doctrine or Rules of those Sciences. And. in Chymistry particularly, ’tis taken for first Constituent and Component Particles of all Bodies, out of which they are made, and into which they arc by Fire, as they say, resolvable again. Thus Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury are the three Famous Chymical Principles, which they call Hypost at leal ; and the Chymists did formerly pretend, that they could by their Art resolve all Natural Bodies into these; and that these Principles could be drawn Simple, Pure, and Uncompoundcd from Metals, Cso But since this Art hath been more commonly studied and consequently much better known, it is found to be a Falsity as Mr. Boyle excellently shews in his Sceptical Chymist ; anti Lemery hints in many places of his good Course of Chymistry. The Modern Chymists agree that there are five kinds, or different Sorts of Bodies, which may by Fire be drawn from many Mix’d Natural Bodies, aud therefore which may in a large sense be called Principles ; as Earth, Salt, Spirit, Phlegm and Oil, tho these can never be drawn perfectly Pure and Unmix’d ; nor have we any reason to believe they are the Constituent Principles of the Bodies they are drawn from ; and out of many Bodies hardly ever a one of them can be drawn ; and therefore they are not truly and properly the Elements or Constituent Principles of Natural Bodies, nor indeed do we know any such. Of these the Spirit, Oyl and Salt, are called the Active Principles ; and the Water and the Earth, the Pastive ones. Mr. Boyle Iheweth by many Experiments in his Sceptical Chymist, in the Discourse about the Producibleness of Chymical Principles, in his Chymical Paradox at the end of his Noctiluca,and in many other places that these Chymical Principles arc Producible and Destructible, and that they arc manifestly Transmutable into one another. For by distilling what the Chymists call Essential Oyl of Aniseeds 36 times over,and some other Oyls of Vegetable above 50 times, he found that there would be Produced above half the first Weight of the Oyl in the form of a Black Pitch That an acid and a volatile Spirit and Salt were to be gained in a considerable quantity ; and upon the whole it appeared that these Resulting Bodies of such very different Forms were produced by the Action of the Fire transmuting part of the very Substance of the Oyl into them. That in general may be called a Principle which is the first cause of any Things Existence, or Production, or of its becoming JQtomt to us. The Aristotelian or Pcripatctical Principles are the Four Elements, Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. The Epicurean Principles, arc Magnitude, Figure, ana Weight. probe.c: PROBE, a Chirurgical Instrument to sound the Depth and Circumstances of Wounds or Ulcers.

problem.c: PROBLEM, is a Proposition which relates to Practice; or which proposes something to be done ; As to make a Circle passe through three given Points not lying in a Right Line : To find the Compaffe, Gse.

procatarctica.c: PROCA1ARCTICA, is the pre-existent Cause of a Disease, which co-oppcrates with others that are subsequent ; whether it be external or internal, as Anger, or Heat in the Air, winch beget ill juice in the Blood and cause a Fever. Blanchard.

procedendq.c: PROCEDENDQ, isa writ whereby a Plea or Cause formerly called from a bale Court ro the Chancery, Kjngs-Bcnch, or Common-Pleas, by Writ of Privilcdge or Ccrtiorari, is released and lent down again to the same Courts to be proceeded in there after it appeared! that the Defendant hath no cause of Privilcdge, or that the matter comprised in the Bill be not well proved.

processe.c: PROCESSE. in Law is the manner of proceeding in every Cause, being the Writs and precepts that go forth upon the Original upon every Action, being either Original or Judicial. Sometimes that only is called the Process, by which a man is called into the Court,because it is the beginning or principal part thereof, by which rhe rest of the business is directed, The difference between Process and Precept, or Warrant of the Justices, is this, she Precept or Warrant is only to attach and convent the party before any Indictment or Conviction, and may be made either in the name of the King or the Justice : But the Process is always in the Kings name, and usually after an Indictment.

process.c: PROCESS, in Chymistry signifies the whole exact Course of any Operation or Exjerimcnt.

procession.c: PROCESSION, in Cathedral and Conventual Churches, the members formerly had their stated Processions, wherein they walked two and two in their most Ornamental Habits, with Hymns, Mustek, and other suitable expressions of Solemnity, and respect to the occasion. In every Pa rish there was a Customary Procession of the Parish Prii st, the Patron of the Church with the Chief Flag, or Holy Banner, and the other Parishioners in Ascension Week., to take a Circuit round the Limits of the Manner, and pray fora Blessing on the Fruits of the Earth. To this we owe our present Custom ot Par amputation, which is still in most places called Processioning, and going in Procession, tho' we have loft the Order, and almost the Devotion, as well as the Pomp and Superstition of it.

processumcontinuando.c: PROCESSUM continuando, is a Writ for the continuance of a l'rocejfe, after the Death of the Chief Justice, or other Justices in the Writ of Oycr and Termincr.

processusstyliformis.c: PROCE SUS Styliformis, or Styloides, is a kind of External Process of the Ossa Temporum, being small and long, having the Horns of the Os Hyoides tyed to it: It is a slender and long Appendix, aud in Infants is Cartilaginous, but in Adult Persons, Bony.

processustfigomaticusoriugalis.c: PROCESSUS Tfigomaticus or Jugalis, is an External Process of the Off a Tcmporum, which runs forwards, and is joined with the Bone of the upper Maxilla, from which juncture is formed that Bridge called, the Zjgoma, reaching from the Eye to the Ear, under which lies the Tendons of the Crotaphite Muscle.

prochainamy.c: PROCLIEIN amy,in Common Law,signifies him that is next of Kin to a Child in his Nonage, and is in that respect allowed by Law to deal for him, in the managing his Affairs, as to be his Guardian, if he hold any Land in Socage, and in Redress of any 'Wrong done to him, and is in the Prosecution ot any Action at Law per Guardianum, where the Plaintiff is an Infant, if per proximum amicum, where the Infant is Defendant.

procidentiaani.c: PROCIDENTIA Ani, is a falling out of the Lower end of the lietturn lntcflinum, and is very usual in Children.

procidentiauteri.c: PROCIDENTIA uteri, is a relaxing of the inner Tunick of the Vagina of the Womb, and was cut off by Physicians formerly, and even still, some think the Womb it self may fall down • but the Ligaments are so strong as to hinder any such Fall. Blar/chard.

proclamation.c: PROCLAMATION, is a Notice publickly given of any thing, whereof the King thinks fit to advertise his Subjects.

proclamationofafine.c: PROCLAMATION of a Fine, is a notice openly and solemnly given at all the Assizes held in the County, within one Year after the engrossing it. And these Proclamations arc made upon Transcripts of the Fine, sent by the Justices of the Common pleas, to the Justices of Assize, and the Justices of Peace. PROC I.AMATION of I(ebelllojg is a Publick Notice given by the Officer, That a Man not appearing upon a Subpœna, nor an Attachment in the Chancery, shall be reputed a Rebel, unless he render himself by a Day assigned in this Writ.

procondyli.c: PROCONDYLI are the Bones of the Fingers next the Back of the Hand.

proconfesso.c: PRO confejfo, in Law, is when upon a Bill exhibited in Chancery, the Defendant appears, upon a Habeas Corpus (which is granted by order) to bring him to the Bar, the Court Assigns him a Day to Answer ; which being expired, and no Answer put in, a second Habeas Corpus is granted, and a further Day assign’d ; by which Day, if he answ er not, the Bill upon the Plaintiffs Motion, shall be taken pro corfejfo, unless cause be shewed by a Day, which the Court usually gives, and for want of inch cause ihcw’d upon Motion, the Substance of the Plaintiff’s Bill shall be decreed, as if it had been contest ed by the Defendant’s Answer.

proctor.c: PROCTOR, is he who undertakes to manage another Man’s Cause in any Court of the Civil or Ecclesiastical Law, for his See.

proctorsoftheclergy.c: PROCTORS of the Clergy, are those who are chosen and appointed to appear for the Cathedral, and other Collegiate Churches; as also for the Common Clergy of every Diocefs at the Parliament, to sit in the Lower-house of Convocation.

procuratory.c: PROCURATORY, is the Instrument by which any Person or Community did constitute or delegate their Proctor or Proctor’s to represent them in any Judicial Court or Cause. 1

prorogue.c: PROROGUE, signifies to prolong, or put off to another Day. The Difference between a Prorogation and an Adjournment, or Continuance of the Parliament, is, That by the Prorogation in open Court, there is a Session; and then such Bills as passed in either House, or both Houses, and had not the Assent to them, must at the next Assembly begin again : For every Session of Parliament is in Law a several Parliament; but if it be but Adjourned or Continued, then there is no Session, and consequently all things continued in the seme. State they were in before the Adjournment.

prosecutor.c: PROSECUTOR, in Law, is he that follows a Cause in another’s Name. See Promoters.

pterigopalatinus.c: PTERIGOPALATINUS, or Sphœnoptcrigopalatinus, is a Muscle of the Gar gar eon, whose former Appellation intimates its Progress and Insertion ; the latter its Origin also. This arises from the Process of the Os Sphxnoides, and descends accord to the length of the Interstice made by the internal Ala of the Os SpUxnoidcs and Musculus Pterigoideus Intcrnus of the lower Jaw ; and becoming Tendinous, marches over the Procejfus Pterigoides, and is Inserted to the Forc-part of the Gargareon. The Tendon of this passes over the Pterigoidal Process, which, like a Pully, gives it a different Power from that of the Sphanopalatinus, tho’ they have both their Origin from the Place. Wherefore, contrary to that, This draws the Gargareon downwards ; which Contrivance in Nature is no less remarkable, than any of those where the like Artifice of a Trodden is made use of. P 1 ER1GOPHARYNGEUS, is a Muscle which arises thin and fieihy from both the Pterigoidal Processes of the OsCnnei forme-, also from thcRoct of the Tongue, and Extremities of th cOsIIyoides; from these places its fleshy Fibres run in a semicircular manner, embracing the superior and back Part of of the glandulous Membrane of the Fauces, where they meet in a middle Line. When this Muscle acts, it brings the middle or back Part of the Fauces towards a Plain, by which means, the Ton sile, together with the rest of the Glandules, are comprest in the Evacuation of their Mucus, to join with the Aliment in its descent into the Stomacl <_ in Deglutition ; and at other times to promote Scr cation, in which this Muscle is the chief Instrument: That the Tonjillæ approach towards each other, is observable, when we inspect these Parts in living Persons.

pterigostapfiilinusinternus.c: PTERIGOSTAPFIILINUS Internus, is a Muscle whith moves the Uvula, arising from a small Protuberance of the Os Sphxnoides, and growing into a small round Tendon, which passes over a small Process, like a Hook, of the Procejfus Pterigoidaus, from thence reverting, it’s inserted into the Fore-part of the Uvula.

Its use is to carry the Blood from the right Ventricle of the Heart to the Lungs, and its Coat is double, like that of the Arteries.

pulmonariavena.c: PULMONARIA Vena, or Arterin Venofa, is a Vessel of the Heart, which discharges it self thro' the left Auricle into the Ventricle of the same side ; for after it has accompanied the "VVind-pipe and Arterin Puhnonaris in all their branchings in the Lungs ; and by its small twigs, has received the Blood out of the Artery, all these twigs are united first into two Trunks (vi%. the Right and Left) afterwards into one, which opens into the left Ventricle of the Heart. This Vein hath no valve in it,. except that at its opening into the left V utricle, where at its Orifice are placed two Membranous Valves, called Mitrales from their form resembling,when joined,something of a Mitre. These arc very strong and firm, to sustain the violent morion of the Blood, and to hinder it from returning back again into this Vein, and to direct its course to the Aorta, whose Orifice opens in the Systole of the Ventricle.

So that in a Medium, whose Elasticity is equal to its Density, all Pulses will be equally swift.

After this, melt the Regule again over a strong Fire in a Crucible, and when "it begins to melt, throw into it, by little and little, three times its weight of Salt-peter ; continue a very strong Fire to keep the Matter in constant Fusion; and when the Fumes are all gone, and the Metal appears bright and clear, cast it into an Iron Mortar greased anti warmed; or else if you don’t value the Crucible, leave it in that to cool, and break the Crucible before ’tis quite cold, and then separate the Regule from its Dross remaining at the top, the Gold will be very pure. There arc several other ways of Purifying Gold, as the Depart and Cementation, which see under those words: But this is the best of all. Red Gold is less valuable, as containing most Copper ; the Yellow is better, and it should remain Yellow while ’tis in the Fire. Purification of Silver, is made in the Coppcl thus : Heat the Coppel gently and by degrees, til! it grow red hot, then cast into it four or five times as much Lead as you design to pur isle Silver : The Lead will soon melt and fill the sides of the Coppel ; then put the Silver into the midst of the melted Lead, and it also will presently melt; then lay Wood all about and over the Coppcl, and blow the Flame so that it may reverberate on the Matter, the Impurities of which, will by this means mix with the Lead, and the Silver will remain pure and unmixed in the middle of the Coppel; and the Lead,mixed with the drossy Parts of the Silver, will lie on the sides like a Scum:ThisScum is to betaken off with a Spoon or other Instrument, and is what is called Litharge, which according to the degree of the Calcination it hath endured, is of divers Colours, and sometimes is called Litharge of Gold, and sometimes Litharge of Silver.

pursue.c: PURSUE, or Purlieu, from the French Pur, i. e. Purus, and Lieu, i. e. Locus, is all that Ground near any Forest, which being anciently made Forest, is afterwards, by Perambulations, severed again from the same, and exempted from that Servitude that was formerly laid upon it: And he that Walketh or Courfeth within that Circuit, is not liable to the Laws and Penalties incurred by them which Hunt within the Precincts of the Forest.

pyramid.c: PYRAMID, in Geometry, is a Solid Figure whose Base is a Polygon, and whose Sides are plain Triangles, their several Tops meeting together in one Point. The Solid Content of A Pyramid, is — to j of the Perpendicular Altitude multiplied by the Base; because a Pyramid is } of a Prism of the same Height and Base. -j j ix Encl. which see also proved under the Word Paraltelopipid (the. lame with Prism, j The superficial Area of a Pyramid, is found by adding the Area of all the Triangles, whereof the the Sides of the Pyramid consist, into one sum : For, the whole external Surface (except the Base) of any Pyramid, is nothing but a System of as many Triangles, as the Pyramid has Sides. If a Pyramid be cut with a Plane Parallel to the Base, the Surface of that Truncated Pyramid comprehended between the Parallel Lines, is found by Subtracting the Surface of the Pyramid cut off from the Surface of the whole Pyramid. Also, the external Surface of a right Pyramid, that stands on a regular Polygon Base, is equal to a Triangle, whose Altitude is equal to the Altitude of one of the Triangles which compose it, and its Base to the whole Circumference of the Base of the Pyramid. Whence therefore the. Surface of a right Cone, (for a Cone is but a Pyramid of infinite Sides) equal to a Triangle, whose Height is the side 0 the Cone, and the Bale equal to the Circumference of the Base of the Cone.
